name: Vera Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we do not sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Vera Bauer, 43, and I help with carpentry and general work on building sites. My partner and two children live with me, and the mortgage takes most of the room in our monthly budget.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you usually do from the time you arrive on site until you go home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I carry sheets and timber, mark cuts, and help fit frames while a more experienced worker checks my measurements. I like the moment a bare room starts looking finished, but the carrying wears my shoulders down and I am still learning the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a tidier order sheet is helpful if it gets the right timber to us. I would still expect the crew to be paid for the hours we are asked to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is lifting, marking and fitting, so a small office shortcut does not take those jobs away by itself. I still worry about our thin savings whenever a site has a slow week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the shifts already offered and ask the supervisor about the next week before leaving the site. If pay is short, I would put off replacing household items that can wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technology sounds small enough to manage on my part of the job. The uncertain shifts feel heavier because we have little money set aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of a normal day would the small change touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the person who sends the material request would spend less time checking it. I would still look at the boards when they arrive because a wrong length can waste the afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and your partner do when one of those slow weeks happens now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We check which bills are due before deciding what can wait. The children still need lunch and school supplies, so we do not have many extras to cut.

say: **I would say** a tidier order sheet helps if it brings the right timber to us.
**I would still expect** our crew to be paid for the hours we work.
do: **Keep taking** the shifts already offered and ask about next week before leaving site.
**Put off replacing** household items that can wait if pay is short.
feel: **The technology sounds manageable**, but uncertain shifts feel heavier with little set aside.
S0.quote: I would still look at the boards when they arrive because a wrong length can waste the afternoon.
fieldNote: **She distinguishes** a modest office shortcut from the lifting and fitting she does.
**A thin cushion** makes ordinary slow weeks more immediate than the AI change.

**I spend** most of my day lifting, marking and fitting, so a small office shortcut does not remove my tasks by itself.
**I have thin savings**, so a slow site week worries me even when AI changes little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office may prepare the delivery list faster, but the crew still needs to check what turns up. I would ask that any new tool be shown to us during paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI might handle some notes or work schedules that I see on the site tablet. I use simple AI tools once in a while, but I do not know whether that would help me keep a job if builders change their staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to show me one useful AI feature on the site tablet and try it with an actual delivery list. I would carry on with my current carpentry shifts while I learned, rather than leave work for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am curious enough to try something after I see it work. I would be uneasy if practice were unpaid, because our household cannot spare the hours or money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to check before trusting a tool with a delivery list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the sizes on its list with the drawing and the opening we measured. If it misses one detail, we could lose time waiting for replacement material.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work might be able to help you learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supervisor usually carries the tablet and knows what the office expects from us. I would ask her to walk through one list at the start of a shift when there is time.

say: **I would say** the office may prepare the delivery list faster, but we still check what arrives.
**I would ask** to see any new tool during paid time so I can learn it on site.
think: **I think** AI might handle some notes or work schedules I see on the site tablet.
**I use AI occasionally**, but I do not know whether it would help me keep my job if staffing changes.
do: **Learn one AI feature** on the site tablet using an actual delivery list.
**Keep working** my carpentry shifts while I learn instead of leaving for a course.
feel: **I am curious** after seeing a tool work, but unpaid practice would strain our household.
S1.quote: I would compare the sizes on its list with the drawing and the opening we measured.
fieldNote: **She uses AI occasionally** and is willing to learn a relevant site feature.
**Paid practice** matters because time away from shifts carries a real household cost.

steps.text: Learn one AI feature on the site tablet using a delivery list
Keep taking carpentry shifts while learning the feature

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the robot part comes later, but the office tasks start changing in 2028. I would not call my site job safe just because I use my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI could make schedules and check measurements better than I do, so those parts of my junior role may disappear first. Carpentry has physical tasks, but there is no promise I will still be hired when the work is reorganised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028, I would ask a skilled worker to let me practise fitting door frames and checking them twice. In 2029, I would ask the supervisor what practical shifts are available and set aside a little from a full week if the bills allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels too quick for me to become a confident carpenter. I would still take the next step I can afford, but I could not promise my partner that the income would hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours fell in 2028, what would change first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop any plans to replace the old sofa and make the children’s school needs the priority. My partner and I would have to speak plainly about the mortgage before we were behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might the three years before robots allow you to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get more practice in practical tasks if a builder has work to offer. I would not assume those three years are guaranteed employment, and I would ask about other local sites if my shifts stopped.

say: **I would say** the robot part comes later, but office tasks change in 2028.
**I would not call** my site job safe just because I use my hands.
think: **I think** AI could make schedules and measurement checks better than I do them now.
**I do physical carpentry**, but hiring changes could affect me before robots arrive.
do: **Practise fitting door frames** with an experienced worker before 2028.
**In 2029, ask** what practical shifts are available and save a little from full-pay weeks if bills allow.
feel: **Two years feels quick** for me to become a confident carpenter.
**I cannot promise** my partner our income will hold, though I can take affordable steps.
S2.quote: I would not call my site job safe just because I use my hands.
fieldNote: **Both dates matter** and hands-on work is not permanently protected.
**The 2029 plan** depends on actual shifts and leaves room for the household bills.
**She is cautious** about local work and will not borrow for training without evidence of openings.

steps.text: Practise fitting door frames with an experienced worker before 2028
In 2029, save a little from full-pay weeks if bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives me time to practise skills I am still weak at. I would also say the years are useful only if builders keep giving juniors real tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take the schedules and measurement notes I sometimes help with by 2031. I expect to learn more by then, but I do not know whether being better at carpentry will mean enough paid work nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise fitting frames with someone checking my work and ask to do one new task each year. In 2032, I would check which jobs are actually open before spending money on a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to improve without rushing into a course I cannot afford. I still feel anxious because our savings would not carry us through a long spell without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a more experienced worker to watch you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask them to check the frame after I fit it and show me where my measurements went wrong. Seeing the mistake on the actual wall is easier for me than reading a page about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would make you pay for a certificate in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a nearby builder to explain what work needs it and whether they hire people with it. If that answer stays vague, I will keep learning on site and hold on to the money.

say: **I would say** five years gives me time to practise skills I am still weak at.
**I would add** that the years help only if builders give juniors real tasks.
think: **I think** AI could take the schedules and measurement notes I sometimes help with by 2031.
**My carpentry may improve**, but I cannot know if that means enough paid work nearby.
do: **Practise fitting frames** with a skilled worker checking my work and add one task each year.
**In 2032, check** actual openings before spending on a certificate.
feel: **Five years gives room** to improve without rushing into an unaffordable course.
**Thin savings** make me anxious about a long spell without wages.
S3.quote: Seeing the mistake on the actual wall is easier for me than reading a page about it.
fieldNote: **She converts warning time** into supervised practice suited to how she learns.
**A certificate is conditional** on a nearby employer naming real work for it.

steps.text: Practise fitting frames with a skilled worker and add one task each year
In 2032, check nearby openings before deciding on a certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade gives a family time to notice the change and talk about it. I would not tell another worker that a longer warning makes any trade safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and measurement notes may be done by AI in 2036, then robots could reach sites in 2039. My children will be older by then, and their needs may cost more or change, so I cannot plan around today’s household exactly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep asking for supervised carpentry tasks in the years before 2036 and see what employers still need. In 2037, my partner and I would talk with our older child about study choices when those choices are close, not choose a job for them now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to learn more than I know today if work is available. The robot date still frightens me some because the mortgage and family needs do not pause while I prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change what your children study now because of this card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not push them toward a particular trade while they are still at school. When the older one chooses subjects, we can look at the real options and ask what they enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years let you do that two years did not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can build skill a little at a time and see how site work changes before paying for training. I still have to make choices for the household along the way, because the longer warning does not cover next month’s bills.

say: **I would say** a decade gives my family time to notice the change and talk about it.
**I would not tell** another worker that a longer warning makes any trade safe forever.
think: **I expect AI** to do planning and measurement notes by 2036, followed by robots at sites in 2039.
**My children** will be older, with needs that may cost more or change by then.
do: **Keep asking** for supervised carpentry tasks before 2036 and watch what employers need.
**In 2037, talk** with my partner and older child about study choices when they are close.
feel: **Ten years is enough** to learn more if work is available.
**The mortgage** does not pause while I prepare for robots.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to learn more than I know today if work is available.
fieldNote: **She welcomes time** to learn without treating delay as a promise of secure work.
**Her children’s later needs** may differ, so she postpones specific education advice.

steps.text: Keep asking for supervised carpentry tasks as employers offer them
In 2037, discuss the older child’s study choices with partner and child

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because two years is little time to improve my skills or build savings. Paid practice with an experienced worker and steady shifts would help more than a course that costs money up front.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want people planning this kind of change to remember that junior workers still need patient teaching before anyone expects them to learn a trade alone. My partner and I do our best to keep the mortgage current, but a few missed shifts would use up our small cushion quickly.

headlineQuote: My partner and I do our best to keep the mortgage current, but a few missed shifts would use up our small cushion quickly.
portrait: Vera is a **43-year-old junior construction worker** supporting her partner and two school-age children.
Her **thin savings** make slow site weeks more urgent than modest AI changes.
She is **steady with new tools** and uses AI occasionally once she sees a purpose.
She wants **supervised practice** and will not assume physical work is permanently safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives little time to improve her skills or build savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practice** with an experienced worker and steady shifts would help more than an upfront course.
